*import Mathlib.CategoryTheory.Equivalence*

```lean
rfl.{u} {α : Sort u} {a : α} : a = a
```
***
`rfl : a = a` is the unique constructor of the equality type. This is the
same as `Eq.refl` except that it takes `a` implicitly instead of explicitly.

This is a more powerful theorem than it may appear at first, because although
the statement of the theorem is `a = a`, Lean will allow anything that is
definitionally equal to that type. So, for instance, `2 + 2 = 4` is proven in
Lean by `rfl`, because both sides are the same up to definitional equality.

***
*import Init.Prelude*

```lean
AlgebraicTopology.DoldKan.Compatibility.equivalence₁_inverse.{u_1, u_2, u_4, u_5, u_6, u_7} {A : Type u_1}
  {A' : Type u_2} {B' : Type u_4} [Category.{u_5, u_1} A] [Category.{u_7, u_2} A'] [Category.{u_6, u_4} B']
  {eA : A ≌ A'} {e' : A' ≌ B'} {F : A ⥤ B'} (hF : eA.functor ⋙ e'.functor ≅ F) :
  (equivalence₁ hF).inverse = e'.inverse ⋙ eA.inverse
```

```lean
rfl.{u} {α : Sort u} {a : α} : a = a
```
***
`rfl : a = a` is the unique constructor of the equality type. This is the
same as `Eq.refl` except that it takes `a` implicitly instead of explicitly.

This is a more powerful theorem than it may appear at first, because although
the statement of the theorem is `a = a`, Lean will allow anything that is
definitionally equal to that type. So, for instance, `2 + 2 = 4` is proven in
Lean by `rfl`, because both sides are the same up to definitional equality.

```lean
rfl.{u} {α : Sort u} {a : α} : a = a
```
***
`rfl : a = a` is the unique constructor of the equality type. This is the
same as `Eq.refl` except that it takes `a` implicitly instead of explicitly.

This is a more powerful theorem than it may appear at first, because although
the statement of the theorem is `a = a`, Lean will allow anything that is
definitionally equal to that type. So, for instance, `2 + 2 = 4` is proven in
Lean by `rfl`, because both sides are the same up to definitional equality.

```lean
AlgebraicTopology.DoldKan.Compatibility.equivalence₂UnitIso_hom_app.{u_1, u_2, u_3, u_4, u_5, u_6, u_7, u_8}
  {A : Type u_1} {A' : Type u_2} {B : Type u_3} {B' : Type u_4} [Category.{u_5, u_1} A] [Category.{u_6, u_2} A']
  [Category.{u_7, u_3} B] [Category.{u_8, u_4} B'] {eA : A ≌ A'} (eB : B ≌ B') {e' : A' ≌ B'} {F : A ⥤ B'}
  (hF : eA.functor ⋙ e'.functor ≅ F) (X : A) :
  (equivalence₂UnitIso eB hF).hom.app X =
    eA.unitIso.hom.app X ≫
      eA.inverse.map (e'.unitIso.hom.app (eA.functor.obj X)) ≫
        eA.inverse.map (e'.inverse.map (hF.hom.app X)) ≫
          eA.inverse.map (e'.inverse.map (eB.counitIso.inv.app (F.obj X)))
```

```lean
CategoryTheory.Functor.map_comp_assoc.{u₁, u₂, u_1, u_2} {C : Type u₁} [Category.{u_1, u₁} C] {D : Type u₂}
  [Category.{u_2, u₂} D] (F : C ⥤ D) {X Y Z : C} (f : X ⟶ Y) (g : Y ⟶ Z) {W : D} (h : F.obj Z ⟶ W) :
  F.map (f ≫ g) ≫ h = F.map f ≫ F.map g ≫ h
```
